User: I'm in the middle of a legal matter and could use some clarity. It's a immigration status review case. I hired Michael Torres at Dowd Legal; we have a hearing at small claims court coming up. The timeline is We're in the early stages; our first hearing is next month.. The other side is the other parent in the custody case. This is in Hennepin County, Minnesota. My status has changed and I need to understand the implications. What should I ask my attorney about how to protect my interests in the settle

ment talks? I want to be prepared for the legal process.
Assistant: You’re asking the right thing — going into settlement talks without knowing the immigration consequences can create big, unexpected risks. Below is a practical checklist of questions and topics to raise with Michael Torres (and, if he’s not an immigration specialist, to an immigration attorney as well), plus documents to bring and negotiation tips so you can protect both your custody and immigration interests.

Confirm basics with your lawy

er first
- Which court exactly is handling the hearing next month (family court, immigration court, small claims, etc.)? (It matters for procedure and remedies.)
- Are you working with Michael Torres at Dowd Legal on both the custody and immigration aspects, or just one? If he isn’t an immigration specialist, can he refer you to one or coordinate with immigration counsel?

Essential questions to ask about immigration consequences of any settlement
- Does this settlement (or any admissions required by it) cr

eate or increase risk of removal, denial of relief, or deportation? How?  
- Could terms of the settlement be used against me in immigration proceedings (e.g., as evidence of abandonment, fraud, or inadmissibility)?  
- If the settlement requires me to agree to anything in writing (admissions, relinquishing parental rights, leaving the country, etc.), what are the immigration consequences?  
- Will accepting or paying child support or agreeing to financial terms affect any pending or future immigration appl

ication (adjustment of status, naturalization, waiver, public charge assessment, etc.)?  
- Will the other party be required to notify immigration authorities or report the settlement to any agency? Is there any risk of ICE/USCIS being notified?  
- If criminal allegations are involved (or could be raised), would any criminal plea, diversion, or admission fall into deportable or inadmissible crimes? (If yes, consult criminal/immigration counsel immediately.)  
- If custody terms include moving the child out

of state or country, how will that affect visa/immigration status, travel, and ability to apply for relief?  
- If the settlement involves relinquishing parental rights or adoption, what impact could that have on any peti­tions based on family relationships (I-130, SIJS, derivative status, etc.)?

Questions about the settlement terms themselves (to protect your interests)
- Can I see any settlement offer in writing and get reasonable time to review it before signing? (Ask for at least a few days so you can

consult immigration counsel.)  
- Can we include a clause stating that the settlement is not an admission of fault? (Non-admission clause)  
- Can we include a confidentiality/non-disclosure clause? If yes, is there any required disclosure to government agencies?  
- Include a mutual release limited to the specific claims — avoid overly broad waivers that could affect future claims or immigration filings.  
- Payment mechanics: how, when, and what happens if the other party fails to pay? (Ask for secure me

chanisms, escrow, or lump-sum if appropriate.)  
- Enforcement and modifications: how will enforcement or modification be handled (court jurisdiction, attorney fees for enforcement)?  
- Will the settlement include attorney-fee shifting (who pays legal fees if one side breaches)?  
- Tax consequences: will any lump-sum payments be taxable? (Ask CPA if needed.)  
- Do any terms require me to waive appeals or other legal rights? If so, what rights exactly?

Questions about preparing for negotiations/hearing
-

What is your negotiation strategy and recommended baseline (minimum acceptable terms) and walk-away point?  
- What evidence will be needed at the hearing or to support your position in settlement talks? (Witnesses, documents, police reports, school records, text messages, financial records, immigration documents.)  
- What is the likely timeline if we don’t settle and proceed to hearing/trial? (Discovery deadlines, pretrial conferences, timeline for appeals.)  
- Are there confidentiality or protective-or

der steps we should take to protect sensitive immigration or family information?  
- What are the possible outcomes (best, likely, worst) and their immigration implications?

If you have or may need immigration relief, ask these
- Are there forms/relief I should consider (e.g., adjustment of status, asylum, cancellation of removal, VAWA, U visa, SIJS, waivers such as I-601/I-601A)? Which ones could be affected by settlement terms?  
- Do I need to preserve evidence for immigration relief (e.g., proof of dom

estic violence, hardship, continuous presence)?  
- If I accept a settlement, will that affect my eligibility for any pending or future immigration petition/waiver?  
- If I’m eligible for a waiver, does the settlement make it harder to get a favorable discretion decision?

Practical documents to bring to your meeting with Michael Torres
- All court paperwork and notices (summons, complaints, hearing notices).  
- Any settlement offers already made in writing or messages discussing settlement.  
- Immigrati

on documents: passport, I-94, visas, any USCIS or EOIR notices or filings, A-number if you have one.  
- Prior custody orders, parenting plans, child support orders, and school/medical records for the child.  
- Police reports, protection orders, medical records, communications (texts, emails) relevant to the dispute.  
- Financial documents (paystubs, bank statements) if support or payments are part of settlement.  
- Any criminal records or pending charges.

Negotiation tactics to discuss with your attorn

ey
- Ask for “time to review” clause so you can get immigration counsel before signing.  
- Insist on non-admission language and narrow releases.  
- If money is involved, secure payment terms (escrow, certified payments, or lien until paid).  
- If custody terms are negotiated, specify exact parenting time, travel permissions, notice requirements for relocation, and dispute-resolution methods (mediation before court).  
- Preserve the right to seek post-settlement relief if new immigration issues emerge (n

arrow waiver language).  
- If you’re vulnerable to deportation, prioritize immigration-safe outcomes over purely financial gains — get immigration counsel involved early.

Other important things to confirm
- If Michael Torres is not an immigration specialist, request a referral to a competent immigration attorney and arrange a joint strategy call/meeting.  
- Ask your attorney to put all settlement offers in writing and to never sign a settlement until you’ve had a chance to review with both your attorney

and (if needed) an immigration lawyer.  
- Request that your attorney notify you promptly of any offers or communications from the other side and explain pros/cons in plain terms.

What to expect at the next hearing (prepare to ask at your appointment)
- Is the hearing a settlement conference, temporary order hearing, or final adjudication? What’s on the agenda?  
- What filings or evidence should we submit in advance?  
- Can the judge order anything immediately that affects immigration (e.g., surrender of

passports, ordering one parent to leave the home)? (If yes, ask how to avoid orders that harm immigration status.)  
- Is there an opportunity to mediate before the hearing?

If you’d like, I can:
- Draft a prioritized list of the top 10 questions you should ask Michael Torres at your next meeting.  
- Draft an email to Michael requesting written settlement offers, time to consult immigration counsel, and confirmation of his experience handling immigration consequences.

Would you like me to draft that ema
il or the short prioritized question list now?
